sources.title: Effect of water activity on the crispiness of a biscuit (Crackerbread): Mechanical and acoustic evaluation
sources.version_or_edition: Published journal article, Food Research International 43(6), July 2010, pp. 1650–1655; DOI identifies the article; no later version noted.

sources.observed_operation: Crackerbread samples equilibrated at aw 0.113–0.98, then punctured with a 5 mm cylindrical probe using an Instron universal testing machine while force and acoustic signals were captured together; crispness descriptors were modeled.

sources.title: Study of the distribution of water within a biscuit during cooling; effect on the checking and the breakage
sources.version_or_edition: Published journal article, Food Chemistry 299 (2019), article 125078; DOI identifies the article; no later version noted.
sources.locator: Publisher article preview (Introduction, Materials/temperature snippets, Conclusions) and PubMed record PMID 31279129 / abstract. Direct publisher open returned HTTP 403 during this stage.
sources.observed_operation: Compared round, thicker biscuits with rectangular, thinner pierced biscuits; used Karl Fischer measurement with automated NIR imaging to monitor moisture distribution during cooling/storage and counted checking/breakage over storage. Reported 210 °C oven setpoint and different oven-exit core temperatures (120 ± 6 °C round; 136 ± 9 °C rectangular).
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: The two shapes had different internal moisture distributions and checking outcomes; round biscuits showed more checking, while thinner pierced rectangles had near-zero checking over the observed period. These are experimental products and process conditions, not universal cooling settings.
sources.applicability: Supports measuring post-bake temperature, moisture gradients, and handling after cooling; suggests product thickness/geometry can matter. It did not establish crispness shelf life for this case. Accessible preview does not disclose a transferable cooling-time/RH setpoint.
sources.retrieval_note: Primary publisher snippets and PubMed metadata/abstract reviewed; no food work performed in this assignment.

sources.title: Evaluation of Market-Available Snack Chip Packaging: Modified Atmosphere Packaging, Water Activity, Mechanical Properties, and Efficiency of Packaging Material Use
sources.version_or_edition: Published journal article, Chemie Ingenieur Technik (2024); DOI identifies the article; no later version noted.
sources.locator: Publisher full text: Materials and Methods §§2.1–2.2; Results §§3.1, 3.3–3.5; Conclusions §4 (Wiley page lines 173–198, 262–268, 295–305, 339–348 in the retrieved representation).
sources.observed_operation: Surveyed 108 commercial snack packs bought around Munich from Dec 2022 to Feb 2023; room-temperature storage/testing at about 23 °C; included pouches and cans and several chip/snack categories. Measured headspace gases, aw, package dimensions/material thickness, and seal seam strength; three seal strips per package were T-peeled.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Most pouches were metallized multilayer biaxially oriented polypropylene; pouch thickness was 40–84 µm, seal widths 0.6–1.9 cm, and the study describes a roughly 2 µm sealant layer in a referenced structure. Only 44/108 products had MAP; pouches showed wide oxygen variation and authors hypothesized weak seals in some builds. Storage RH was not stated for the purchased packs. Film WVTR cited in the paper is tied to 23 °C/85% RH; it is not a universal package value.
sources.applicability: Useful real-market packaging/implementation history: package construction, condition and seam properties can vary together and a visually complete pouch does not establish barrier performance. Mixed products, cross-sectional sampling, unknown individual storage histories, and hypothesized causes prevent transferring its conclusions as diagnosis.
sources.retrieval_note: Primary publisher full text reviewed. No inference about the cooperative’s bags beyond testable questions.

critic_independent_review.status: primary publisher full text independently reviewed
critic_independent_review.locator: Materials and Methods §§2.1–2.2 and Results; 108 Munich snack packages bought Dec 2022–Feb 2023, stored/tested about 23 °C, measured water activity, package dimensions/thickness and T-peel seam strength. sources.version_or_edition: Published journal article, Jurnal Teknologi dan Industri Pangan 24(2), published 2013-12-27; DOI identifies the article.

sources.observed_operation: Made a formulation from 60% corn flour/40% glutinous rice flour; measured crispness/hardness and a moisture-sorption isotherm, fit with a Hasley model; used a critical-moisture shelf-life approach for a metallized-plastic package.

authors: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces article authors (publisher record reviewed)
sources.version_or_edition: Published ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces article (2022; DOI identifies article; no revision id noted).

sources.title: Packaging design for potato chips
sources.version_or_edition: Published journal article, Journal of Food Engineering 47(3), February 2001, pp. 211–215; DOI identifies the article.
sources.locator: Publisher article abstract and Materials/Introduction preview; direct publisher open returned HTTP 403 during this stage.
sources.observed_operation: Modeled potato-chip oxidation and moisture/texture change for two commercial multilayers: PP laminated with metallized PP and PVDC-coated PE laminated film. The simulated bag used 400 cm² area, 1,435 cm³ headspace and 65 g product; varied initial nitrogen/water-vapor headspace composition.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Predicted effects depended on whether lipid oxidation or moisture-related loss of crispness was the limiting failure. Replacing pure nitrogen with nitrogen/water-vapor mixtures over 0.1–32% RH was projected to extend modeled shelf life only in conditions where oxidation dominated; moisture-driven crispness could worsen.
sources.applicability: Useful design-history evidence that alternative headspace strategies are failure-mode dependent and cannot be selected without knowing formulation and quality-limiting mechanism. This snack’s composition and rancidity history are unknown, so MAP modification is not a provisional path.
sources.retrieval_note: Primary publisher abstract and methods preview; any numerical result is a model projection, not a measured cooperative outcome.

critic_independent_review.status: carried primary-publisher note reviewed; full article not independently reopened
critic_independent_review.locator: Carried note describes a modeled potato-chip/headspace comparison and the oxidation-versus-moisture tradeoff. The draft explicitly defers MAP absent oxidation evidence.

sources.title: Effects of process parameters and solid particle contaminants on the seal strength of low-density polyethylene-based flexible food packaging films
sources.version_or_edition: First published 2021-03-17; Packaging Technology and Science 34(7), pp. 413–421; DOI identifies the published article.
sources.locator: Wiley full text: Abstract, Materials and Methods §§2.1–2.2.4, Results/Conclusions §§3–4 (retrieved lines 118–176, 218–253, 273–276).
sources.observed_operation: Compared four 50 µm PE-based industrial films (LDPE and LLDPE/mLLDPE blends) using hot-tack and T-peel methods. Specimens were conditioned 24 h at 23 °C/50% RH. Hot tack used 1 s/0.8 bar and an additional 0.5 s comparison; contamination tests used coffee (~200 µm) and powdered sugar (~30 µm) across flat/grooved bars and multiple temperatures/contaminant densities.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Composition and seal-bar geometry affected seal initiation/strength. At 0.5-s dwell, reported coffee contaminant threshold was about 10 g/m² while powdered sugar threshold was 2 g/m². At 1 s, 4 g/m² did not significantly affect tested strength. The effect depends on particle type, loading, geometry and dwell; article cautions that seal-bar geometry may also produce leak-prone weak regions.
sources.applicability: Supports recording snack fragments/crumbs at the seal, material construction, seal-bar condition and actual process window. The studied PE films and settings are not the cooperative's unknown multilayer; do not prescribe any of these settings or thresholds.
sources.retrieval_note: Primary Wiley full text reviewed. Published lab seal tests, not cooperative production evidence.

critic_independent_review.status: primary Wiley full text independently reviewed
critic_independent_review.locator: Abstract, Methods, Results §§3.5–3.6, Conclusions: PE compound-film tests; coffee/sugar particle sizes, bar geometry; 0.5 s thresholds about 10 and 2 g/m²; at 1 s, 4 g/m² was not significant. Study settings are not transferable.

sources.title: Effect of Liquid Contamination on Hermeticity and Seal Strength of Flexible Pouches with LLDPE
sources.version_or_edition: Journal of Applied Packaging Research 9(1), Article 5 (2017); institutional repository full-text record; no DOI shown.
sources.locator: Rochester Institute of Technology repository abstract; methods/results summary and recommended citation (lines 13–32 in retrieved representation).
sources.observed_operation: Tested flexible HFFS pouches with LLDPE sealant, with control, salt-water and vegetable-oil contamination at the fin/end-seal T-point; varied sealing temperatures and dwell times; compared refrigerated and ambient storage over 14 days.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: For the study setup, 140 °C/0.3 s was reported as optimal; salt-water contamination had a lower hermeticity pass rate in Phase 1, while the abstract reports no significant category difference in seal strength across 14 days and no overall contaminant effect under its tested conditions.

sources.title: Shelf-life simulation of packaged rice crackers
sources.version_or_edition: Published article, Journal of Food Quality 32(2) (2009), pp. 224–239; first published 2009-04-02; DOI identifies the article.
sources.locator: Wiley full text: Methods, sensory panel, experimental shelf-life and model-validation sections (retrieved lines 105–126, 128–141, 174–218).
sources.observed_operation: Compared two rice-cracker formulations (initial moisture 4.12% vs 2.28%; fat 1.87% vs 21.09%) in PE and PP pouches. Used 20 g/package, impulse-sealed, six replicates, and storage at 30 °C/75% or 85% RH. A 10-person trained panel rated sensory texture; aw was measured daily to product-specific cutoffs. Measured package WVTR and fit GAB sorption/model predictions.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Each product had a distinct critical aw (0.43 ± 0.01 and 0.39 ± 0.02). Model fit was closer to experiment for RC-1 (R² 0.90) than RC-2 (R² 0.51); it overpredicted RC-2 shelf-life, suggesting sorption/permeability alone missed product structure/moisture migration. Higher RH shortened observed time to endpoint; PP performed better than PE in tested pouches.
sources.applicability: Strong example of linking initial moisture, product-specific sensory cutoff, actual pouch material and storage RH; also a concrete caution about simulation error. All numerical cutoffs/durations remain product-specific, not the cooperative’s shelf-life evidence.
sources.retrieval_note: Primary Wiley full text reviewed; study calculations/results belong to the article and were not recomputed here.

critic_independent_review.status: primary Wiley article abstract and metadata independently reviewed; carried methods note also reviewed
critic_independent_review.locator: Abstract: two formulations, PE/PP pouches, 30 °C/75% and 85% RH; validation fit R² 0.90 and 0.51, showing model limitations for one product. Study-specific values are not transferred.
